title: Work email in work repos, personal email everywhere else — automatically
summary: Setting the right identity per repository works right up until you forget once. Conditional includes make git choose by directory, so the wrong email becomes impossible rather than unlikely.
mental_model: `[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]` pulls in another config file when the repository lives under that path. It is evaluated per repository, at read time, so the identity follows the directory rather than your memory.

steps.title: One identity for everything
steps.why: Both repositories resolve to the global identity, because nothing distinguishes them. Commit in the work repository now and it carries your personal email — permanently, in the commit object.
steps.expect: The same personal email in both.

verify.label: the work repository is currently using the personal identity

steps.title: Write the work identity into its own file
steps.why: A separate config file holds everything work-specific: identity, signing key, whatever else differs. Keeping it separate is what makes the include readable a year later.

write.content:
[user]
	name = Work Name
	email = you@company.example
[commit]
	gpgsign = false

steps.expect: A small file with just the work-specific settings.

steps.title: Include it conditionally
steps.why: `includeIf gitdir:` matches on the repository's path. The trailing slash matters — it means 'this directory and everything under it'. A pattern that does not start with `~/`, `./` or `/` gets `**/` prepended, so `gitdir:work/` matches any repository under a directory called work — which is also the only form that behaves identically on Windows and Unix. In your own dotfiles you would normally write the absolute `gitdir:~/work/`.
steps.expect: The work repository now resolves to the company email; the personal one is unchanged.

verify.label: the work repository picked up the work identity automatically
…and the personal one was left alone

steps.title: Prove it at commit time
steps.why: Config resolution is not a display trick — the identity is baked into the commit. Commit in each repository and read the author back.
steps.expect: Two commits, two identities, no thinking required.

verify.label: the work commit carries the work email
the personal commit carries the personal email

steps.title: See where each value came from
steps.why: `--show-origin` names the file behind every value, including included ones. When an identity is not what you expect, this ends the investigation in one command.
commands: sh -c 'cd work/service && git config --list --show-origin --show-scope | grep user'
sh -c 'cd personal/sideproject && git config --list --show-origin --show-scope | grep user'
steps.expect: The work repository citing gitconfig-work; the personal one citing the global file.

steps.title: Match on the remote instead of the path
steps.why: `hasconfig:remote.*.url` matches on where the repository points rather than where it sits — the right condition when work repositories are scattered across your disk. It needs git 2.36 or newer.
steps.expect: The condition is recorded; the personal repository is unaffected because its remote does not match.

steps.title: Close the last gap
steps.why: Conditional includes only help inside the directories you configured. `user.useConfigOnly true` makes git refuse to commit anywhere it has no configured identity, instead of inventing one from your hostname — the two settings together make a wrong email genuinely impossible.
commands: sh -c 'cd personal/sideproject && git config --get user.email || echo "no identity — git will refuse to commit here"'
steps.expect: The work repository still resolves; the personal one now has no identity at all, and git will say so rather than guess.

verify.label: git will refuse to guess an identity
the conditional include still supplies the work identity
the work repository commits with the work identity
verify.hint: [includeIf "gitdir:<path>/work/"] pointing at a work config file

verify.label: the personal repository commits with the personal identity
both a path-based and a remote-based condition are configured
git refuses to invent an identity where none is configured

pitfalls: The trailing slash in `gitdir:~/work/` matters: without it the pattern matches the directory itself and not repositories inside it.
`gitdir` is case-sensitive on Unix. Use `gitdir/i:` when the path's case varies, which it does on Windows and macOS.
Conditional includes apply to the repository's own path, not your current directory. A worktree elsewhere on disk resolves against the worktree's location.
The include only fires when git reads config for that repository — a repository you clone outside the configured directory silently gets the global identity.
`user.useConfigOnly true` is the safety net that turns 'wrong email' into an error message. Set it once and forget it.
cheatsheet: the file to pull in when it matches
match by remote instead of path
